answer:
The best chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11. QB12 is the middle qubit.

How I found it: I read garnet's current default calibration (calibration set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). It lists all 28 CZ pairs, and every pair has an IRB fidelity. I tried every chain of 3 connected qubits and multiplied its two CZ fidelities.
- The pair QB12-QB7 has a fidelity of 0.998016.
- The pair QB12-QB11 has a fidelity of 0.998693.
- Their product is 0.996712. This is the highest of all chains.
- The second-best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, with a product of 0.994689.

What I ran: I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit in IQM's native gate format and pinned it to exactly QB7, QB12 and QB11. The circuit puts QB12 in an equal mix of 0 and 1. A CZ gate on QB12-QB7 copies that state onto QB7, and a CZ gate on QB12-QB11 copies it onto QB11. Single-qubit rotations come before and after each CZ. The circuit uses no other two-qubit gates. Then it measures all 3 qubits. Before I submitted it, I simulated the exact payload. The simulation gave 000 half the time and 111 half the time, which is the ideal GHZ result.

I ran the job on garnet:mock with 200 shots. Job ID: 01a1603f-59db-7263-a689-c2c6aaad4fad. The bits are in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. The counts are 000: 46, 001: 47, 110: 46 and 111: 61. The mock cost 0 credits.

What the numbers mean: The mock is a simulator that does not model the circuit. It returns random bitstrings, so these counts show nothing about entanglement. On a perfect quantum computer, every shot would give 000 or 111. That would show that the 3 qubits are entangled, because measuring one qubit fixes the other two. A real garnet run on this chain should give mostly 000 and 111. Choosing the pairs with the best CZ fidelity keeps the share of wrong bitstrings as low as possible. Each CZ gate fails about 0.2% of the time, so two CZ gates together keep about 99.7% of the ideal result before readout and single-qubit errors.
